analysis.one_liner: Requires every employer to offer every worker a pension as good as what federal employees get.
analysis.headline: The Pensions for All Act, which would put every private worker into a federal-style pension, was introduced on February 12, 2026 and referred to three House committees, where no action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every employer in the country to give each employee a retirement plan with benefits equal to the federal employees' pension system — or simply enroll workers in that federal system, FERS. Employers and self-employed people would have to contribute a share of pay (with reduced amounts for small employers and lower-income self-employed people), face a $10-per-day tax for noncompliance, and get a tax credit of up to half their contributions if they are small. Employers would be barred from cutting existing pay to cover the cost.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people without an employer pension — especially employees of retail, food service, and small businesses where 401(k) coverage is rare — gain a guaranteed-benefit, employer-funded pension with a survivor and disability benefit, plus a Thrift Savings Plan account. Small employers and self-employed people who comply receive a tax credit covering up to half their contributions.

how_it_helps.text: Every employee would have a retirement plan with a guaranteed lifetime annuity benefit and employer contributions comparable to what federal employees get, instead of the current system where many workers have only an optional 401(k) with no employer match.

Employees would keep the Thrift Savings Plan account they built, since moving to or from a covered employer is treated as staying in the same system, and account balances transfer rather than being stranded.

Small employers and self-employed people get a tax credit of up to 50 percent of required pension contributions, phasing down as receipts or income rise, which lowers the burden for the smallest businesses.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost: mandatory contributions to the federal pension fund (with a 50 percent reduction for small employers, rising for larger firms based on revenue), the Thrift Savings Plan match, and a $10-per-employee-per-day tax for failing to comply, with joint liability across commonly-owned businesses. Self-employed people owe their own contributions, with credits phasing out as income rises above $75,000.

drawbacks.text: The employer contribution requirement — roughly half the normal employer share, rising with firm size — is a new mandated cost of employment, which businesses argue would be especially hard for low-margin industries; Section 7 forbids employers from cutting other pay to cover it, which does not eliminate the pressure [S2].

Employers whose existing plans are not certified as FERS-comparable would have to join FERS or redesign their plans, and the bill's effective date reaches plan years after December 31, 2025, which could disrupt retirement arrangements already in place [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is substantial: a mandatory employer-funded pension with a survivor benefit and an inflation-protected annuity, instead of the voluntary 401(k) system that many employees never participate in. The cost falls on employers, particularly larger ones, as a new payroll obligation, though small employers and self-employed people get tax credits worth up to half their contributions, and the smallest employers pay only half the standard employer share. The main good-faith objections are the administrative burden of enrolling every private employer in or alongside the federal retirement system, the possibility that employers would offset the cost through wage growth, and the effective-date language covering plans already in place, which could disrupt existing retirement arrangements.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to three House committees in February 2026, and no committee has taken it up since, so it sits with no scheduled action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on February 12, 2026 [S1], [S4].
It was referred the same day to the Ways and Means, Oversight and Government Reform, and Education and Workforce Committees [S4].
It has 11 cosponsors, all House Democrats, and no action has been taken on it since the referral [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that would bear the new pension mandate benefit from the bill going nowhere; no one has gained anything yet because the bill has not been enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoiding the mandate, for now

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican cosponsor has joined, and the bill sits in committees controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.industry: Employers with no retirement plan (retail, food service, small firms)
industries.note: These employers would bear new mandatory pension contributions and a $10-per-employee-per-day tax for noncompliance, softened by a 50 percent reduction for firms with revenue up to $25 million and tax credits. Their workers gain a real pension.

industries.industry: Retirement plan administration and investment management (401(k) industry)
industries.note: A federal FERS-equivalent default could shrink the market for employer-sponsored 401(k) administration and mutual fund fee revenue among employers that elect FERS instead of a private plan.

industries.industry: Federal retirement trust funds (Civil Service Retirement and Disability Fund, Thrift Savings Fund)
industries.note: The funds would gain millions of new contributors and the government would gain a new administrative role as the default retirement system for the private sector, with new compliance responsibilities for the Labor Department and Treasury.

analysis.trajectory: With 11 cosponsors, no Republican support, and referral to three committees under a Republican majority, the bill is unlikely to receive a markup or a floor vote; most bills referred to multiple committees at this stage never advance.
